scope: Proposed evidence/falsification work plan only; no claims externally verified, no editorial/rights decisions or release authority.

items.original_sentence:
Abstract
​This repository contains the primary dataset and forensic reconstruction of a Universal Metric Invariant (13.7g) that functioned as the "Hard-Coded" standard for Bronze Age trade between the Indus Valley Civilization and the Levant.
items.proposed_treatment: Reframe the universal 13.7g trade standard as a hypothesis explored by this notebook, not an established archaeological fact.
items.evidence_plan: Obtain independently dated Indus and Levant weight catalogs; define unit classification, sample selection, chronology, and alternative standards.
items.falsification_question: Do independently sourced mass distributions and dates support a shared 13.7g unit better than separate local standards?
items.quantitative_or_control_check: Compare distributions against multiple candidate units and controls; report uncertainty and exclusions.

items.original_sentence:
Forensic Case Study: The Eshtemoa Silver Hoard
​The Eshtemoa Hoard (Judean Highlands) contains five jugs filled with over 26kg of "Hacksilber" (cut silver).
items.proposed_treatment: Attribute the five-jug/over-26kg claim to a verified excavation inventory or label these numbers unverified.
items.evidence_plan: Locate original Eshtemoa excavation inventory with vessel and aggregate mass measurements; cite page, edition and unit conversions.
items.falsification_question: Do primary find records actually establish five jugs and more than 26kg, rather than a later retelling?
items.quantitative_or_control_check: Reconcile counts and total mass against original itemized inventory.

items.original_sentence:
​The 13.7g Calibration: When the data is re-calculated using the Indus 13.7g Standard, the "scraps" resolve into perfect fractions:
​6.85g (The Beqa/Half-Unit)
​3.42g (The Quarter-Unit)
​The Conclusion: The silver was physically "hacked" to satisfy the requirements of a Registry that demanded the 13.7g Indus standard.
items.proposed_treatment: Separate 13.7/2 = 6.85 and 13.7/4 = 3.425 arithmetic from the unsupported claim that silver was deliberately cut to these values.
items.evidence_plan: Collect measured fragment masses and analytical precision; distinguish arithmetic fractions from observed archaeological cutting practices.
items.falsification_question: Could 13.7g fractions fit only because a base was selected after seeing the data?
items.quantitative_or_control_check: Compare 13.7/2=6.85 and 13.7/4=3.425 with raw measurements, alternative bases and null distribution; state rounding rule.

items.original_sentence: The Result: When you use the 13.7g weight to calibrate the water flow, the clock perfectly predicts when the Moon will disappear and reappear.
items.proposed_treatment: Reframe the claimed perfect lunar prediction as a proposed experiment, not a demonstrated result.
items.evidence_plan: Specify water-clock dimensions, rate stability, dates, calibration and independent lunar ephemeris before examining results.
items.falsification_question: Would held-out eclipse or lunar-event predictions be no better than a simple calendar baseline?
items.quantitative_or_control_check: Pre-register out-of-sample dates, prediction error and baseline comparisons.

items.original_sentence: ​The Registry Solution: The "Crossers" enforced the 13.7g standard so that 1 unit of Indigo matched 1 unit of Silver.
items.proposed_treatment: Label the indigo/silver one-to-one registry rule as speculative reconstruction, not an attested historical transaction.
items.evidence_plan: Find contemporaneous indigo/silver contracts, accounting units and independent provenance for the asserted one-to-one registry rule.
items.falsification_question: Do attested transactions show variable units, prices or no such registry?
items.quantitative_or_control_check: Compare units of mass, value, commodity grade and conversion assumptions before any 1:1 statement.

items.original_sentence: * The Calibration: If you take a 13.7g chert weight to the top of the High Island salt dome, the "Metric Friction" changes slightly compared to sea level.
items.proposed_treatment: Frame salt-dome balance differences as a testable physical hypothesis, not demonstrated ancient calibration.
items.evidence_plan: Define what a salt-dome experiment would measure and whether an ancient balance could resolve the effect.
items.falsification_question: Is the expected gravity-induced weight change below measurement resolution, or unrelated to an ancient calibration practice?
items.quantitative_or_control_check: Distinguish invariant mass from local weight; calculate expected delta and instrument uncertainty.

items.original_sentence: In the Registry, these are the "Grounding Pins." A 13.7g silver jar buried in a salt dome doesn't just sit there; it is protected from electromagnetic "noise," preserving the Metric Purity of the metal for thousands of years.
items.proposed_treatment: Qualify or remove the salt-dome shielding and millennia-long metric-purity preservation claim pending physical evidence.
items.evidence_plan: Define proposed shielding and metal-preservation mechanism; seek physical tests and independently sourced archaeological observations.
items.falsification_question: Does salt-dome burial fail to attenuate the relevant fields or fail to preserve metal relative to controls?
items.quantitative_or_control_check: Specify field strength/frequency, corrosion controls, measured endpoints and time scales.
